articles.title: How Glass rebuilds nested generic type names
articles.excerpt: Decompile a type nested inside a generic type and the name you get back — Outer .Inner — looks nothing like the name stored on disk. The metadata holds Inner1`, with a backtick and a number, and that…
articles.body: Decompile a type nested inside a generic type and the name you get back — Outer<int, string>.Inner<bool> — looks nothing like the name stored on disk. The metadata holds Inner 1`, with a backtick and a number, and that number is not three, even though three type parameters are in scope inside the type. The gap between those two spellings is one of the small, precise things a decompiler has to get exactly right, because getting it wrong produces C# that does not compile. The real question A generic type name in .NET metadata is mangled: List 1 , Dictionary 2 , Func 4`. The backtick and the number encode the type's generic arity . That rule is simple until types nest.
articles.author: Zero Heartbeat

articles.title: You Sent the Delivery Note Photos at Low Detail and the Model Read a Thumbnail
articles.excerpt: The drivers photographed A model read each photo In testing In the first week live Then the complaints came. Quantities wrong. Batch codes invented. A handwritten "2 bags split" Same model. Same promp…
articles.body: The drivers photographed every signed delivery note. A model read each photo and pulled out the order number, the quantities, and any note about damage. In testing it was excellent. In the first week live the cost was lower than planned. Then the complaints came. Quantities wrong. Batch codes invented. A handwritten "2 bags split" read as "2 bags". Same model. Same prompt. Nothing in the response said the photo was unclear. Every field came back filled in, with the same confidence as before. Here is the mechanism. The image call had one extra field: "detail": "low" Someone had added it to save money. On OpenAI's API, low detail does not mean "look a little less carefully". It means the model receives one small copy of the image, 512 pixels by 512. A fixed, small number of tokens.
articles.author: Serguey Asael Shinder

articles.title: Rotate a JPEG four times with jpegtran -perfect and the MD5 comes back identical
articles.excerpt: When a product photo for a small shop site comes in sideways, the obvious fix is to open the file, rotate it and hit save. That save is a full decode and re-encode, and it happens again whenever someo…
articles.body: When a product photo for a small shop site comes in sideways, the obvious fix is to open the file, rotate it and hit save. That save is a full decode and re-encode, and it happens again whenever someone straightens or trims the same photo later. A test on 2026-11-18 put a number on that cost. A 1200×672 JPEG at quality 85 was turned 90° twenty times, two ways. Decoding, rotating and saving at quality 85 each round ended at 37.81 dB PSNR and 0.9932 SSIM against the starting file, with the pixels changed. jpegtran -rotate 90 -perfect twenty times left every pixel identical to the start, and the file was still 275,220 bytes. This is one photo on one Apple silicon Mac, each chain run once, so read every figure below as "on this image".

articles.title: Liberties, ko and two passes: how I coded the rules of Go in about 360 lines of JavaScript
articles.excerpt: Go has the shortest rulebook of any board game I've built. Place a stone, capture a group by taking its last liberty, don't repeat a position, and the bigger area wins. Getting those few rules exactly…
articles.body: Go has the shortest rulebook of any board game I've built. Place a stone, capture a group by taking its last liberty, don't repeat a position, and the bigger area wins. Getting those few rules exactly right still took more care than the postcard version suggests. Go is one of the 60+ games on mympgames , my free multiplayer browser arcade. It runs on 9×9, 13×13 and 19×19 boards. The whole rules engine is one file, go-rules.js , and that same file runs in two places: on the server, which decides what's legal, and in a Web Worker in the browser, where the computer opponent thinks. This post follows one stone from the moment you click to the moment the game is scored. The code is real, trimmed a little. The board is a flat array of numbers No classes, no Stone objects.

articles.title: One Laptop Sending Headers Slowly Took Your Go Server Down
articles.excerpt: The stock service Fast. Simple. One line started it: http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux) It ran for two years. Then one afternoon CPU was low. Memory was fine. The log said Here is the mechanism. Someon…
articles.body: The stock service was a small Go binary. Fast. Simple. One line started it: http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux) It ran for two years. Then one afternoon it stopped answering. CPU was low. Memory was fine. The log said http: Accept error, too many open files. Here is the mechanism. Someone had opened a few thousand connections. On each one they started an HTTP request. And never finished the headers. A few bytes. Wait ten seconds. A few more bytes. The server was patient. It kept every connection open, waiting politely for the blank line that ends the headers. It never came. Each connection held a file descriptor. The process had a limit on those. When the limit was reached, real customers could not connect at all. The attack has a name. Slowloris. Robert Hansen published it in 2009.

articles.title: Why Vampire Survivors Started on Phaser and JavaScript: The Web Stack Behind Bullet Heaven — And Why It Had to Leave
articles.excerpt: Vampire Survivors should not have been a Steam hit. A browser-first 2D framework, JavaScript garbage collection, and thousands of bats on screen is a recipe for lag — yet a tiny prototype built by une…
articles.body: Vampire Survivors should not have been a Steam hit. A browser-first 2D framework, JavaScript garbage collection, and thousands of bats on screen is a recipe for lag — yet a tiny prototype built by unemployed developer Luca Galante became the defining bullet-heaven of 2022, won Best Game at the BAFTAs, and spawned a whole genre of Survivors-likes. The short answer for developers is this: Galante built Vampire Survivors in 2020-2021 with Phaser, the 2D HTML5 game framework , shipped it as a free browser game and then as a cheap Steam Early Access title, and only later ported it to Unity at version 1.6 to fix performance and reach consoles. That two-act engine story is the lesson — but my take is different from most postmortems: the port was not proof that Phaser failed.

articles.title: An AI agent can already read Siemens TIA Portal. Writing back is where it breaks.
articles.excerpt: An AI agent can already open a Siemens TIA Portal project and read it: block interfaces, hardware tree, tag tables, the SCL inside each FB. That part is solved — Siemens Openness has been scriptable f…
articles.body: An AI agent can already open a Siemens TIA Portal project and read it: block interfaces, hardware tree, tag tables, the SCL inside each FB. That part is solved — Siemens Openness has been scriptable for years, and wrapping it in MCP takes a weekend. Writing back is where it falls apart. Not because the model writes bad SCL, but because five specific things go wrong the first time an agent touches a live engineering project, and none of them are visible in a chat window. If you're building this — an MCP server for PLC tooling, or a gateway like the one we maintain — these are the failures to design against from the start, in the order we hit them. 1. Structure is not data, and OPC UA only gives you data The reflex is to read through the PLC: OPC UA, browse the tag tree, done.

articles.title: Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation
articles.excerpt: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its stellar companion.
articles.body: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports. As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now. "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean.
